content: Patients were treated with the recommended dose of cefdinir capsules, which is 600 mg per day. The majority of adverse events observed were mild in nature and self-limiting. There were no reported deaths or permanent disabilities attributed to cefdinir therapy. Among 5093 patients, 147 individuals (3%) discontinued the medication due to adverse events that investigators considered possibly, probably, or definitely related to cefdinir treatment. The primary reasons for discontinuation were gastrointestinal disturbances, most commonly diarrhea or nausea. Additionally, 4% of patients discontinued the medication due to rashes thought to be associated with cefdinir administration. During postmarketing surveillance, which began after cefdinir's approval in Japan in 1991, various adverse experiences and altered laboratory test results have been reported, regardless of their direct relationship to cefdinir. These include severe reactions such as shock, anaphylaxis (with rare cases of fatality), facial and laryngeal edema, and a sensation of suffocation. Other reported conditions include serum sickness-like reactions, conjunctivitis, stomatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, exfoliative dermatitis, erythema multiforme, erythema nodosum, acute hepatitis, cholestasis, fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure, jaundice, increased amylase levels, acute enterocolitis, bloody diarrhea, hemorrhagic colitis, melena, pseudomembranous colitis, pancytopenia, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic anemia, acute respiratory failure, asthmatic attacks, drug-induced pneumonia, eosinophilic pneumonia, idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, fever, acute renal failure, nephropathy, bleeding tendencies, coagulation disorders, disseminated intravascular coagulation, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcers, ileus, loss of consciousness, allergic vasculitis, potential cefdinir-diclofenac interaction, cardiac failure, chest pain, myocardial infarction, hypertension, involuntary movements, and rhabdomyolysis. Adverse events associated with cephalosporin-class antibiotics in general have also been reported. These include allergic reactions, anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, toxic epidermal necrolysis, renal dysfunction, toxic nephropathy, hepatic dysfunction (including cholestasis), aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, hemorrhage, false-positive tests for urinary glucose, neutropenia, pancytopenia, and agranulocytosis. Symptoms of pseudomembranous colitis may occur during or after antibiotic treatment (refer to Warnings). Several cephalosporins have been implicated in triggering seizures, particularly in patients with renal impairment when the dosage was not appropriately reduced (refer to Dosage and Administration and Overdosage). If seizures associated with drug therapy occur, the medication should be discontinued. Anticonvulsant therapy may be administered if clinically indicated.
